Taiwanese 16-tile mahjong, with the rules of southern Taiwan, of a family table or the full tai table, and every rule adjustable. The computer players and the analysis use a neural network trained by self-play: in practice you can see hints as you play; afterwards, review a hand move by move to see what went well and what didn\'t; or set up any position and see what each choice is worth. Open source (GPLv3).

Which decisions a review stops at as mistakes:
• Beginner: blunders (a loss of about 0.5 tai or more)
• Intermediate: mistakes (about 0.25 tai or more)
• Expert: questionable moves too (about 0.1 tai or more)
The thresholds scale with the rules' tai; within 0.05 tai counts as equally good.

On a win, each losing player pays base + tai to the winner. The base is counted in tai: base 2 is 2 tai. Simple 1 has 2; the others 1.
On a draw, the dealer keeps the deal.\n• On: the dealer streak goes up by one\n• Off: the streak stays as it is
When several players can win on the same discard:\n• On: they all win, and the discarder pays each of them\n• Off: only the first of them in turn after the discarder wins
The tiles left in the wall, never drawn (usually 16). When only these are left and no one has won, the hand is a draw.
The fewest tai a win needs (dealer tai aside). 0: a hand with no tai can win.
• Off: single wait counts only if the whole hand waited on one tile.\n• On: it counts if the winning tile can be read as an edge, inside or pair wait, even with other waits too.

• 0 No flowers: 136 tiles.\n• 1 Every flower: 144 tiles; every flower counts.\n• 2 Seat flowers: 144 tiles; only your seat\'s flowers count (East: Spring, Plum; South: Summer, Orchid; West: Autumn, Chrysanthemum; North: Winter, Bamboo), and a full set counts as a flower set.
Tai for each flower that counts: every flower you get, or with seat flowers, your seat\'s two.
Flower set: tai for each full set, Spring to Winter or Plum to Bamboo (seat flowers only).
All eight flowers: a player with all 8 flowers wins at once, as a self-draw (all three others pay); only these tai, dealer tai and the base count. 0: no such win.
Seven rob one: when a player has 7 flowers and another gets the 8th, the one with 7 wins at once, and the one with the 8th pays as on a deal-in. 0: no such win.
Dealer tai. When the dealer wins, each losing player pays these tai more; when someone else wins, the dealer pays these more if the dealer is paying.
Dealer streak: tai added to the dealer tai for each hand the dealer keeps the deal.\n• 1: a streak of 1 is 2 tai in all; of 2, 3 tai\n• 2: a streak of 1 is 3 tai in all; of 2, 5 tai
Concealed hand: a win with no chow, pung, exposed kong or added kong (concealed kongs are fine).
Self-draw: you drew the winning tile yourself.
Concealed self-draw: tai added for a concealed hand that self-draws. Concealed 1 + self-draw 1 + this 1 = 3 tai.
Single wait: a win waiting on one tile only (edge, inside or pair wait). How strictly it\'s judged: Loose single wait.

All chows:
• All five sets are chows; the pair is suited
• No honors and no flowers in the whole hand
• A win on a discard (not a self-draw), on a two-sided wait that isn't a single wait
Counts together with concealed hand.
Fully melded: all five sets chowed, punged or konged on the table, one tile left in hand as a pair wait, winning on a discard.
Whether fully melded also counts single wait. On: both count (Masters 2 + 1 = 3 tai).
Melded self-draw: all five sets on the table as in fully melded, but winning by self-draw (self-draw and single wait count as usual).
Round wind: a pung (or kong) of the round\'s wind.
Seat wind: a pung (or kong) of your seat\'s wind. When the round and seat winds are the same, both count.
Dragon pung: each pung (or kong) of Red, Green or White.
Little three dragons: two dragons as pungs and the third as the pair. Those two pungs don\'t also count as dragon pungs.
Big three dragons: pungs of all three dragons. They don\'t also count as dragon pungs.
Little four winds: three winds as pungs and the fourth as the pair. Round and seat wind count as usual.
Big four winds: pungs of all four winds.
Whether round wind and seat wind still count with big four winds.
All pungs: all five sets are pungs (or kongs), no chows.
Three concealed pungs: three pungs made in hand (or concealed kongs). A pung made with someone\'s discard isn\'t concealed.
Four concealed pungs: four of them. Three concealed pungs no longer counts.
Five concealed pungs: five of them. Three and four concealed pungs no longer count.
Half flush: one suit only, plus honors.
Full flush: one suit only, no honors.
All honors: the whole hand is honors. All pungs, wind and dragon tai count as usual.
Robbing a kong: winning on the tile someone adds to a kong (they pay as on a deal-in). At 0 you can still rob a kong, with no tai for it.
Win after kong: self-drawing the replacement tile after a flower, concealed kong or added kong (not an exposed kong). At 0 it counts as a plain self-draw.
Last tile: self-drawing the last tile that can be drawn. Doesn\'t count together with win after kong.
Last discard: winning on the last tile discarded.
Heavenly hand: the dealer wins on the deal, before the first discard (and any kong). Concealed hand and self-draw no longer count.
Earthly hand: a non-dealer self-draws on their first draw, with no chow, pung or kong before it. Concealed hand and self-draw no longer count.
Human hand: a non-dealer wins on someone\'s discard before their own first discard, with no chow, pung or kong before it. Concealed hand no longer counts.

Heavenly ready: ready and declared before your first discard, with no chow, pung or kong before it (the dealer, or a non-dealer ready with the 16 dealt tiles).\n• After declaring, you only discard what you draw, or win; no chow, pung or exposed kong. A concealed kong is allowed if the waits stay the same.\n• These tai are added on a win; at 0 it can\'t be declared.

Declared ready: with a concealed hand (concealed kongs allowed) that is ready, declare it as you discard; the discard must leave the hand ready.
• After declaring, you only discard what you draw, or win; no chow, pung or exposed kong. A concealed kong is allowed if the waits stay the same.
• These tai are added on a win; at 0 it can't be declared (0 in every preset).
• On your first discard, heavenly or earthly ready counts instead when it applies.

Earthly ready: a non-dealer ready and declared with their first discard, after their first draw, with no chow, pung or kong before it.\n• After declaring, you only discard what you draw, or win; no chow, pung or exposed kong. A concealed kong is allowed if the waits stay the same.\n• These tai are added on a win; at 0 it can\'t be declared.
Wind pung: every wind pung counts, in place of round wind and seat wind (an option of the every-flower, every-honor style).
No honors, no flowers: the whole hand has no honors and no flowers (an option of the every-flower, every-honor style).
Exposed kong: each exposed or added kong counts (an option of the every-flower, every-honor style).
Concealed kong: each concealed kong counts (an option of the every-flower, every-honor style).
Taiwanese 16-tile mahjong: the tiles, calls, ready hands and tai, explained with the rules you choose.
Taiwanese mahjong is played a little differently from place to place. Choose one way; the pages on flowers, tai and scoring follow it, and you can switch there to see the difference at once.
This choice is for this guide only. Practice uses Settings → Rules; the last page can apply it there.
Everyone holds 16 tiles. On your turn, draw one and discard one. Make five sets and a pair, 17 tiles, and you win.
A set is a chow (three in a row of one suit) or a pung (three of a kind); the pair is two of a kind.
Four of a kind is a kong, also one set; after a kong you draw one more tile from the wall to keep your hand complete.
Three suits, Characters, Dots and Bamboo, each 1 to 9; honors are the four winds, East, South, West and North, and the three dragons, Red, Green and White. Four of each, 136 tiles.
No flowers with these rules: the 136 tiles are all.

Plus 8 flowers: Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter, Plum, Orchid, Chrysanthemum and Bamboo, 144 tiles. Flowers make no sets: one you get is laid on the table and replaced from the end of the wall, all by itself.
Every flower: each flower is %1$s tai.

Seat flowers: only your seat\'s flowers count, %1$s tai each (East: Spring, Plum; South: Summer, Orchid; West: Autumn, Chrysanthemum; North: Winter, Bamboo). A full set, Spring to Winter or Plum to Bamboo, adds %2$s tai.
Flower wins: a player with all 8 flowers, or with 7 when another gets the 8th (who then pays), wins at once: %1$s tai.
The dealer starts with 17 tiles and discards one. Then the next player (on the right) draws one and discards one, and so on around the table.
You can take a tile someone discards:
Chow: only from the player on your left, with two tiles in hand to make a run.
Pung: from anyone, with two of the same in hand.
Kong: with three in hand, take the fourth when discarded (exposed kong); draw the fourth yourself (concealed kong); or draw the fourth for a pung on the table (added kong). Then draw a replacement.
Win: when someone\'s discard completes your hand; the discarder deals in. Winning with a tile you drew is a self-draw.
Chowed, punged and konged sets go face up on the table (melds); then you discard.
When several players want a tile: win first, then pung or kong, then chow.
When several can win on a discard (%1$s): only the first of them in turn after the discarder wins.
When several can win on a discard (%1$s): they all win, and the discarder pays each of them.
The last %1$d tiles of the wall are never drawn. When only they are left and no one has won, the hand is a draw: no one gains or pays.
Each player\'s discards lie in order in front of them: their river. Its marks:
Draw-discard: the tile just drawn, thrown at once. An orange face.
Claimed: taken by another player\'s chow, pung or kong. At a real table it leaves the river; here it stays, darker, to keep the order.
A claimed draw-discard: a deeper orange.
A blue bar on the left: the first discard after that player\'s chow, pung or kong.
How they tell whether an opponent is close to ready: Table tips, in the settings.
A hand one tile from winning is ready; the tiles that would complete it are its waits. Common waits:
Two-sided: either end of a run.
Pair: one tile to make the pair.
Dual pung: two pairs, either one making a pung.
Waiting on one tile only (edge, inside or pair) is a single wait: %2$s tai more with these rules (%1$s).
Waiting on one tile only (edge, inside or pair) is a single wait: no extra tai with these rules (%1$s).
Passing a win: if you could win and didn\'t, you can\'t win until your next discard.
On a win, each losing player pays base + tai to the winner. With these rules the base is %1$s tai.
Self-draw: all three others pay. A win on a discard: only the discarder pays.
Dealer: when the dealer wins or pays, add %1$s dealer tai, and %2$s more for each hand of the dealer\'s streak (a streak of 1: %3$s tai).
For example, a non-dealer self-draws with only self-draw, %1$s tai: the other two non-dealers pay %2$s tai each, the dealer pays dealer tai too, %3$s tai, and the winner gets %4$s tai in all.
Concealed self-draw: concealed hand (%1$s) + self-draw (%2$s) + bonus (%3$s) = %4$s tai.
A hand with no tai can win.
A win needs at least %1$s tai (dealer tai aside).
On a draw no one gains or pays; the dealer keeps the deal and the streak goes up by one.
On a draw no one gains or pays; the dealer keeps the deal and the streak stays.
When the dealer wins, the dealer deals again; when someone else wins, the next player deals. When everyone has dealt, a round is over (East Round, South Round…); four rounds are a full game.
This hand is ready. Tap the tiles you think it wins on, then Check.
Green: right; red: not a win; dashed: missed.
6-7 Bamboo waits on 5 or 8 Bamboo: two-sided. You hold two 8 Bamboo, but 8 still wins.
2-3-4 Characters with 5 as the pair wait, or 3-4-5 with 2 as the pair wait: 2 or 5 Characters.
3-4-5 with 6-7 waits on 5 or 8; 3-4 with 5-6-7 waits on 2 or 5. In all: 2, 5 or 8 Characters, a three-sided wait.

When an opponent looks ready (many melds, several discards straight from the draw) and you are two or more away, or fewer than 20 tiles are left: throw their own discards first, then honors already seen and suji; an unseen non-suji middle tile is the most dangerous.
Both keep you just as fast: throw the safe one.
When the improving tiles are about even, throw the tile that is safe against whoever may be ready.
You are %1$s with %2$d tiles left; falling back with %3$s only slows you down.

Close to ready, your chance to win outweighs the risk: even against an opponent who is 90% ready, the neural network falls back only about 20% of the time one away, under 10% when ready; it folds often only with fewer than 10 tiles left.
Keep the pair of %1$s and throw %2$s (%3$s).
%2$d more %1$s are unseen: you can pung one from any of three players, or keep the pair as the eye; %3$s waits on one kind, which you must draw or chow from the player before you.
The improving tiles are about even, but a pair can be punged from any of three players and serves as the eye; without it a hand often lacks one.
%1$s does little for the hand; the pair of %2$s can still be punged (%3$d unseen) and serves as the eye.

A call that brings you closer: the neural network makes it almost always with 40 or more tiles left, about half the time with 11 to 25, about 20% with 10 or fewer.

This %1$s does not pay: %2$s after it, %3$s without, one step faster; but with three fewer tiles in hand you deal in more often, and win no more often.
This %1$s does not pay: %2$s after it and %2$s without, no faster; with three fewer tiles in hand fewer draws help, and you win less often.

One to three away, the neural network pungs an honor pair 30 to 50% of the time even when it gets no closer, and almost always when it does.

Early, with three or more tiles to win on, the neural network often passes on a discard to wait for a self-draw (about half the time with 40 or more tiles left); with fewer than 25 left it almost always wins.

Is an opponent ready, when to fall back, which tile is safer: from 200,000 hands of self-play.

An orange face is a draw-discard; a darker tile was claimed by another player, a deeper orange one was a claimed draw-discard; an inset blue bar on the left marks the first discard after a chow or pung. Players throwing draw-discards in a row or who just called are often ready.
Count their discards and melds. The table shows how often players who look like this are really ready; with the last two or more straight from the draw, about half as much again.
With an opponent who looks 60 to 80% ready, how often the neural network turns to safety (a step back, or as fast but safer): mostly by the tiles left and your own distance.

Against a player who is ready, how often each kind of tile deals in. Their own discards are nearly safe; suji about halve it; an honor already seen once is safe; an unseen non-suji middle tile is the most dangerous.
The last three columns (2 seen, 1 seen, None seen) are non-suji tiles.
A 4 to 6 with suji on one side only (half-suji): %1$s.
From 200,000 hands of the built-in neural network playing itself (Simple 2, Every flower); other rules are much the same.
In a review, a decision that lost points (or beat tile efficiency) has an Explain button.
Throwing %1$s puts you a step further from ready (%2$s → %3$s); %4$s does not.
After throwing %1$s, %2$d improving tiles move you forward; after %3$s only %4$d.
Keep your distance from ready first, then keep the most improving tiles; on a tie throw honors and terminals first.
A step back for a better hand
%1$s is faster (%2$s), but the neural network would rather throw %3$s and be a step slower (%4$s): what stays wins bigger or comes together more easily.
" From what they have thrown, the neural network thinks they are more likely ready than that."
" From what they have thrown, the neural network thinks they are less likely ready than that."
Both leave you ready; %1$s is the safer throw.
The wait after throwing %1$s wins more often: more of its tiles are still in the wall, or others throw them more readily.

%1$s and %2$s keep about as many improving tiles (%3$d against %4$d), but the neural network clearly prefers %1$s: the difference is in how the hand develops (which partial sets fill more easily, how safe the tiles kept are).
From the wall and partial sets to shanten and suji
The shuffled tiles on the table that nobody has drawn yet. The players draw from it in turn; \"N tiles left\" counts what can still be drawn.
The tiles you hold, hidden from the others: 16 as a rule; on your turn you draw a 17th from the wall and discard one.
The tiles each player has discarded, in order, laid out in front of them. A player\'s river hints at what they wait for and which tiles are safe against them.
One go-around of the four players, each drawing and discarding once: by the 8th turn each has discarded about 8 tiles. The first few are the early turns.
Characters (萬), dots (筒) and bamboo (條), each numbered 1 to 9, four of each tile.
The four winds (east, south, west, north) and the three dragons (red, green, white): seven kinds, four of each. They have no numbers to run in a sequence.
The 1s and 9s of the number suits, together with the honors. A 1 or a 9 runs only one way (1-2-3, 7-8-9) and an honor not at all, so they are harder to use and often go first in the early turns.
The 2s to 8s of the number suits: they run both ways, so they are the most useful (4, 5 and 6 most of all), and for the same reason the likeliest to be waited on, the riskiest to discard.
Three numbers in a row of one suit, such as 4-5-6 of characters.
Three of the same tile, such as three east winds or three 5 dots.

Four of the same tile. After a kong you draw a replacement from the wall, to keep enough tiles. A kong with another player\'s discard is open (明槓); one of four tiles you drew yourself is concealed (暗槓).
A chow or a pung (a kong counts as a pung): a finished group of tiles.
The pair that goes with five sets to make a complete set of tiles.
Five sets and an eye, 17 tiles in all, make a win, and the deal ends. The last tile may be one you draw or another player\'s discard.
Winning on a tile you draw yourself; all three others pay.
Discarding the tile another player wins on; only the one who dealt in pays.
Nobody has won when the wall runs out (but for the tiles always left unplayed): nobody pays.
From the shuffle and the deal until someone wins or the wall runs out: one hand.
One tile from a win; the tiles that would complete it are your waits. Some rules let a player declare it (報聽).
The scoring unit: a win counts up tai for what it holds, and each payer pays a base plus the tai.
The player who draws and discards first in a hand. When the dealer wins, or pays, the dealer\'s tai is added.
The dealer keeps the deal after winning or after an exhaustive draw. Each time adds to the dealer\'s tai (in the simple rules, one tai more each time).
When the dealer does not keep the deal it passes to the next player; once all four have dealt, a round ends (the east round, the south round, …), and four rounds make a game (一將).
The eight flower tiles (seasons and plants). One drawn is shown at once and replaced from the wall; it is part of no set, and by the rules may add tai.

Taking the tile another player just discarded to make a set, shown on the table: a chow (only from the player before you), a pung or an open kong (from anyone). A pung shown so takes the fourth tile when you draw it (an added kong). Sets shown so are melds.
One discard or one decision (which tile, whether to call, whether to win). The review counts moves; a hand is the whole deal.
A hand without a chow, pung, open or added kong (a concealed kong is fine). By the rules a concealed win may add tai, a concealed self-draw more.
Letting a win go (passing on a discard, or not declaring a self-draw). Until you next discard (or declare a concealed or added kong) you cannot win at all, on a discard or on your own draw.
Two tiles one short of a set, such as 4-5 or 4-6 of characters, or a pair.
A tile that joins nothing else in the hand and has no pair.
A partial chow open at both ends, such as 4-5 of characters: a 3 or a 6 completes it, the easiest to complete.
A partial chow missing its middle, such as 4-6 of characters: only a 5 completes it.
A partial chow at the end of a suit: 1-2 (only a 3 completes it) or 8-9 (only a 7).
Ready with five sets done and one tile left, waiting for its match to make the eye.
Ready with two pairs: a third tile of either wins, that pair becoming a pung and the other the eye.
A pair whose other two tiles are already on the table: it can never become a pung, only the eye or be broken.
How many right tiles a hand is from ready: one away needs one more, two away two.
The tiles that would bring a hand closer to ready (or, when ready, win), counted as the copies not yet seen on the table.
Playing for speed alone, ignoring danger and tai: the fewest away first, then the most improving tiles.
Discarding the tile just drawn: the orange tiles in a river. A player who does it several times in a row often needs nothing more and may be ready.
Discarding a tile already in the hand and keeping the one drawn: the river\'s ordinary tiles.
A tile a player has discarded is, against that player, one of their own discards. Taiwanese rules let them still win on it, but it deals in under 1% of the time: the safest tiles.

A number tile three away from one an opponent discarded, in the same suit: after their 4, the 1 and the 7 (a 4, 5 or 6 needs both sides: a 4 after their 1 and 7). Against them it deals in a third to a half as often as a like tile with none seen on the table.
Against an opponent, a number tile that is not their own discard, with no suji on either side (a 4 when they discarded neither the 1 nor the 7): the riskiest kind.
A 4, 5 or 6 with suji on one side only (a 4 when they discarded the 1 but not the 7): riskier than suji, safer than non-suji.
A tile none of whose copies has appeared on the table (rivers and melds). Late in a hand these deal in most.
A tile with copies already on the table. The more seen, the less likely anyone holds a pair of it waiting; an honor with one seen is very safe.
